title: Hardware Support
subtitle: 20 questions across cables, motherboards, RAM, storage and RAID, power, and printers

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Anti-Static Bag

questions.q: USB 3.0 (3.2 Gen 1) ports are color-coded blue and run at what maximum speed?
questions.note: USB 3.0 = blue port, 5 Gbps. USB 2.0 = black, 480 Mbps.

explain.correct: USB 3.0 / 3.2 Gen 1 operates at 5 Gbps and uses a blue port to visually distinguish it from USB 2.0.
wrong: 480 Mbps is USB 2.0 speed, not USB 3.0.
10 Gbps is USB 3.1 / 3.2 Gen 2, one generation faster.
40 Gbps is USB4 or Thunderbolt 3/4 -- not USB 3.0.

questions.q: Which video connector carries NO audio signal?
questions.note: VGA is analog video only; it has no audio pins. DVI is also audio-free.

explain.correct: VGA is an analog video-only standard; it has no provision for audio. HDMI and DisplayPort both carry audio.
wrong: HDMI carries multi-channel audio alongside video.
DisplayPort carries audio and is commonly used with monitors that have built-in speakers.
USB-C in Alt Mode (DisplayPort or Thunderbolt) can carry audio as part of the protocol.

questions.q: A technician installs a CPU with pins on the chip itself. Which socket type is this?
questions.note: PGA = pins on the CPU (AMD AM4). LGA = pins on the motherboard (Intel).

explain.correct: PGA (Pin Grid Array) has the pins on the CPU package. AMD AM4 uses PGA. If you bend a pin, you damaged the CPU.
wrong: LGA (Land Grid Array) has the pins on the motherboard socket, not the CPU -- Intel's design.
BGA (Ball Grid Array) is soldered directly to the board; it has no removable pins and is non-upgradeable.
ZIF-LGA is not a standard socket designation used in CompTIA A+ curriculum.

questions.q: A PC powered off overnight now shows a 'CMOS checksum error' and the system clock reset to January 1, 2000. What is the most likely cause?
questions.note: Dead CR2032 CMOS battery causes BIOS settings -- including the clock -- to reset on every power cycle.

explain.correct: The CMOS battery (typically a CR2032 coin cell) maintains BIOS/UEFI settings and the real-time clock when power is removed. A dead battery causes settings to revert and the clock to reset.
wrong: A failed hard drive causes boot failures or read errors, not a CMOS checksum error or clock reset.
A corrupted bootloader would prevent the OS from loading, but BIOS POST settings and the clock would remain intact.
Faulty RAM causes POST failures, blue screens, or memory errors -- not CMOS checksum or clock issues.

questions.q: How many pins does a DDR4 desktop DIMM have, and at what voltage does it operate?
questions.note: DDR4 DIMM = 288 pins, 1.2V. DDR3 = 240 pins, 1.5V. SO-DIMM DDR4 = 260 pins.

explain.correct: DDR4 desktop DIMMs have 288 pins and operate at 1.2V, lower than DDR3's 1.5V, reducing power consumption.
wrong: 240 pins / 1.5V is DDR3, not DDR4. Both values are wrong for DDR4.
260 pins is the SO-DIMM DDR4 laptop form factor, not the full-size desktop DIMM.
288 pins is correct but 1.5V is the DDR3 voltage; DDR4 drops to 1.2V.

questions.q: Which RAID level uses dual parity and can survive the simultaneous failure of TWO drives?
questions.note: RAID 6 = two independent parity blocks per stripe, tolerates any two drive failures.

explain.correct: RAID 6 writes two independent parity sets across all drives, allowing it to continue operating even if two drives fail simultaneously.
wrong: RAID 1 mirrors two drives and can survive one failure, but uses no parity and cannot survive two failures.
RAID 5 has single distributed parity and can only survive one drive failure.
RAID 10 mirrors pairs then stripes them; it can survive one failure per mirrored pair, but two failures in the same mirrored pair are catastrophic.

questions.q: What is the approximate maximum sequential read speed of a SATA III solid-state drive?
questions.note: SATA III = 6 Gbps link, real throughput ~550 MB/s. NVMe Gen3 reaches ~3500 MB/s.

explain.correct: SATA III's 6 Gbps interface limits real-world SSD sequential reads to roughly 550 MB/s due to protocol overhead.
wrong: 3500 MB/s is the approximate ceiling for NVMe Gen 3, which bypasses the SATA controller entirely.
300 MB/s is closer to SATA II era performance limits.
150 MB/s was typical of SATA I spinning hard drives, not modern SSDs.

questions.q: A laser printer leaves toner on the page but it smears when touched. Which component is most likely failing?
questions.note: The fuser (~200 C) permanently melts toner into the paper. If toner smears, the fuser is not reaching temperature.

explain.correct: The fuser assembly uses heat (~200 C) and pressure to permanently bond toner to the paper. Smearing means toner was transferred but never fused.
wrong: The imaging drum holds the electrostatic image. A failing drum causes lines or ghost images, not smearing.
The primary corona wire charges the drum surface. A failure here causes blank or all-black pages, not smearing.
The transfer belt or roller moves toner from drum to paper. A failure causes missing toner, not unfused smearing.

questions.q: Which NVMe M.2 key and size designation is most commonly used for SSDs in modern desktop and laptop builds?
questions.note: M.2 2280 Key M is the standard 22 mm wide by 80 mm long NVMe SSD form factor.

explain.correct: M.2 2280 (22 mm wide, 80 mm long) with Key M is the dominant NVMe SSD size. The M key supports PCIe x4 needed for NVMe speeds.
wrong: M.2 2230 Key A+E is the 30 mm long form factor used for Wi-Fi cards, not primary storage drives.
M.2 3042 is not a standard consumer SSD designation in the CompTIA A+ curriculum.
M.2 2242 is only 42 mm long and used in some industrial or compact devices; it is not the dominant consumer form factor.

questions.q: What port number does IPP (Internet Printing Protocol) use?
questions.note: IPP = port 631. Port 9100 = raw/JetDirect. Port 515 = LPD/LPR.

explain.correct: IPP (Internet Printing Protocol) uses TCP port 631. It is the modern standard used by CUPS and most network printers.
wrong: Port 515 is LPD/LPR (Line Printer Daemon/Remote), an older UNIX printing protocol.
Port 9100 is raw printing (JetDirect / AppSocket), used for direct byte-stream print jobs.
Port 443 is HTTPS; it is not a printing protocol port.

questions.q: Which PSU rail provides the majority of wattage to the CPU and discrete GPU?
questions.note: +12V delivers the highest wattage; modern CPUs and GPUs draw almost entirely from this rail.

explain.correct: The +12V rail supplies the bulk of power in a modern system, driving the CPU (via EPS connector) and GPU (via PCIe power connectors).
wrong: +3.3V powers low-voltage logic on the motherboard and some DIMM slots; it carries far less wattage.
+5V powers USB ports, some storage drives, and legacy components; it is not the dominant rail for CPU/GPU.
-12V is a legacy rail used for serial ports and some audio cards; it carries only a fraction of a watt in modern systems.

questions.q: What is the correct NAND flash endurance ranking from MOST to LEAST durable?
questions.note: SLC stores 1 bit per cell (most writes before wear-out). QLC stores 4 bits (cheapest, lowest endurance).

explain.correct: SLC (1 bit/cell) has the highest endurance, followed by MLC (2), TLC (3), and QLC (4). More bits per cell means more write stress and shorter lifespan.
wrong: This is the reverse order -- QLC is the least durable, not most durable.
SLC, not MLC, is the most durable. This order incorrectly demotes SLC.
TLC is not more durable than SLC or MLC; it stores more bits per cell at the cost of endurance.

questions.q: Which UPS type provides zero transfer time during a power failure because it runs the load through its inverter continuously?
questions.note: Online double-conversion UPS: AC -> DC -> AC continuously. No switchover delay. Cleanest power.

explain.correct: An online double-conversion UPS converts AC to DC and back to AC continuously, so the load always runs from the inverter. There is literally zero transfer time during a utility failure.
wrong: A standby (offline) UPS runs loads from utility power and only switches to battery when power fails; there is a brief switchover delay (typically 2-10 ms).
A surge protector with battery backup is a marketing term; it typically behaves like a standby UPS at best and has a measurable transfer time.
A line-interactive UPS adds an AVR transformer for voltage regulation but still switches to battery during an outage, introducing a short transfer time.

questions.q: Dual-channel memory doubles theoretical bandwidth. What physical requirement must be met to enable dual-channel mode on most motherboards?
options: Enable XMP in BIOS after installing any two sticks
Install two DIMMs of any speed in any slots
Install a matched pair of DIMMs in the A2 and B2 slots (same-colored slots)
questions.note: Matched pair in same-color (A2/B2 or A1/B1) slots enables dual-channel. Mismatched slots force single-channel.

explain.correct: Most motherboards require a matched pair (same capacity, ideally same speed) installed in the correct paired slots -- typically A2 and B2 (or A1 and B1) -- to activate dual-channel mode.
wrong: ECC memory is for error correction, not channel configuration. ECC DIMMs do not by themselves enable dual-channel.
XMP enables faster rated speeds but does not enable dual-channel; proper slot placement is required regardless of XMP.
Installing two DIMMs in any slots does not guarantee dual-channel; slots must be from different channels (A and B).

questions.q: A POST card inserted into an expansion slot displays hex code 'C1'. What is this device testing?
options: The phase of POST where a failure occurred
questions.note: POST diagnostic cards output 2-digit hex codes to pinpoint which POST phase failed, before video output is available.

explain.correct: A POST card monitors the diagnostic port (I/O port 80h) and displays the two-hex-digit code the BIOS last wrote, identifying which initialization phase failed -- useful when no video output is available.
wrong: SMART attribute checks are performed by drive firmware and reported via OS tools; not by POST cards.
CPU thermal output is monitored by BIOS hardware sensors or tools like HWMonitor, not POST cards.
POST cards do not test network connectivity; that is an OS-level function or a loopback adapter test.

questions.q: Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4 both use which physical connector and share what maximum bandwidth?
questions.note: Thunderbolt 3 and 4 both use the USB-C physical connector and deliver 40 Gbps bidirectional bandwidth.

explain.correct: Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4 use the USB-C physical connector and both support 40 Gbps. TB4 adds stricter minimum feature requirements compared to TB3.
wrong: Mini DisplayPort was the connector for Thunderbolt 1 and 2, not Thunderbolt 3/4.
USB-A is a rectangular legacy connector; Thunderbolt 3/4 use USB-C, not USB-A.
USB-C connector is correct but 80 Gbps applies to Thunderbolt 5, not Thunderbolt 3 or 4.

questions.q: Which storage technology should NEVER be defragmented, and what maintenance command does Windows use instead?
options: NVMe drive; run a full format monthly
SSD; run TRIM (Optimize Drives uses TRIM automatically)
questions.note: Defragmenting an SSD wastes write cycles without benefit. Windows Optimize Drives issues TRIM on SSDs instead.

explain.correct: SSDs have no moving parts, so defragmentation offers no performance benefit and wastes the limited P/E write cycles. Windows Optimize Drives detects SSDs and sends TRIM commands instead of defragmenting.
wrong: NVMe drives are a type of SSD and should also never be defragmented, but a full monthly format is never the correct recommendation.
Optical discs cannot be defragmented or TRIM-ed; they are read-only or rewritable sequential media.
Magnetic HDDs benefit from defragmentation because read heads must physically seek across the platter; defragmenting HDDs is correct, not avoided.

questions.q: BIOS/MBR partition tables have two key limitations compared to UEFI/GPT. What are they?
options: Max 4 TB disk, max 8 primary partitions
Max 2 TB disk, max 128 primary partitions
Max 1 TB disk, max 2 primary partitions
Max 2 TB disk, max 4 primary partitions
questions.note: MBR caps at 2 TB and 4 primary partitions. GPT supports disks well beyond 2 TB and up to 128 partitions (Windows default).

explain.correct: The MBR partition table uses 32-bit LBA addressing, limiting disks to 2 TB, and only supports 4 primary partitions. GPT removes both restrictions.
wrong: 4 TB and 8 partitions are both incorrect for MBR. GPT supports very large disks; MBR is limited to 2 TB and 4 partitions.
2 TB is correct but 128 partitions applies to GPT, not MBR. MBR allows only 4 primary partitions.
1 TB is incorrect; MBR's 32-bit LBA limit caps addressable space at 2 TB, not 1 TB.

questions.q: An inkjet printer from Epson uses precisely controlled pressure to eject droplets without heat. What technology does this describe?
questions.note: Piezoelectric inkjet (Epson) uses a crystal that deforms under voltage. Thermal inkjet (HP, Canon) vaporizes ink with heat.

explain.correct: Piezoelectric inkjet technology uses a piezoelectric crystal behind each nozzle. Applying voltage deforms the crystal, which mechanically ejects a droplet -- no heat required. Epson uses this approach.
wrong: Thermal inkjet (used by HP and Canon) heats ink to form a vapor bubble that forces a droplet out. It uses heat, not mechanical pressure.
Electrophotographic (laser) printing uses static electricity and toner powder, not liquid ink.
Direct thermal printing uses heat-sensitive paper and no ink at all; it is used for receipts and fax machines.

questions.q: AHCI and NVMe both allow SSDs to operate, but they differ dramatically in command queue depth. What are the respective queue depths?
questions.note: AHCI has a single command queue with a depth of 32 entries (NCQ). NVMe supports up to 65,535 queues with 65,535 entries each.

explain.correct: AHCI provides one command queue with up to 32 entries (NCQ), enough for the single-threaded access pattern of spinning hard drives. NVMe supports 65,535 parallel queues each with up to 65,535 commands, eliminating the queuing bottleneck for flash storage.
wrong: AHCI has a single command queue, not 256. The NVMe figure of 65,535 is correct, but the AHCI number is not.
AHCI has one queue (32-deep), not 32 queues, and NVMe supports 65,535 queues, not 1,024 - both halves are wrong.
AHCI has one command queue with 32 entries (NCQ), not 32 separate queues. The 65,535 NVMe figure is correct, but the AHCI characterization is not.
